q-124301:
An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

First, notice that we can express the given transformation as

$$
[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6u-v \\ 2u-3v+4\end{aligned}].
$$

Separating the constants and expressing the linear part as a product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}6u-v \\ 2u-3v+4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6u-v \\ 2u-3v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}6 & -1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=6+(-3)+4=7.
$$

q-20963:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 8 & 16 & -8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-8){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x+2y=-1 \\ 0x+0y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x+2y=-1.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=-1-2y,$ and the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1-2y \\ y=y\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1-2y \\ y\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

q-73750:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 4 \\ -3 & 6 & -12\end{aligned}]
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 4 \\ -3 & 6 & -12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-2y=4 \\ 0x+0y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x-2y=4.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=4+2y,$ and the general solution is

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=4+2y \\ y=y\end{aligned}
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4+2y \\ y\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-130923:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 \\ -4 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 \\ -4 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
{\begin{aligned}x-2y=-1 \\ 0x+0y=3.\end{aligned}
$$

However, the final equation $0x+0y=3$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=3,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

q-91033:
The given operator is a second-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={a}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{a}_{1}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{a}_{0}y
$$

with constant coefficients  ${a}_{2}=1,{a}_{1}=-2,$ and ${a}_{0}=0.$ 

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D(y) & =D(\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =(\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x})(\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-2(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

q-337831:
The given operator is a second-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={a}_{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{a}_{1}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{a}_{0}y
$$

with constant coefficients  ${a}_{2}=1,{a}_{1}=2,$ and ${a}_{0}=-5.$ 

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}D(y) & =D(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)) \\  & =(\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}-5)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) \\  & =\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))-5\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))+2\cdot (3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) \\  & =-9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) \\  & =-14\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+6\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\end{aligned}
$$

q-65037:
The given operator is a second-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y
$$

with ${f}_{2}=x,{f}_{1}=2,$ and ${f}_{0}=0.$

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D(y) & =D(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =(x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x})\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{x})+\frac{2}{x} \\  & =x\cdot (-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})+\frac{2}{x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{2}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

q-91045:
The given operator is a third-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={f}_{3}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+{f}_{2}(x)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x)y.
$$

with ${f}_{3}={x}^{2},{f}_{2}=-2x,{f}_{1}=x,$ and ${f}_{0}=0.$

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}D(y) & =D({x}^{4}) \\  & =({x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}-2x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}){x}^{4} \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}({x}^{4})-2x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}({x}^{4})+x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{4}) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(4{x}^{3})-2x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(4{x}^{3})+x(4{x}^{3}) \\  & ={x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(12{x}^{2})-2x(12{x}^{2})+4{x}^{4} \\  & ={x}^{2}(24x)-24{x}^{3}+4{x}^{4} \\  & =24{x}^{3}-24{x}^{3}+4{x}^{4} \\  & =4{x}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

q-337848:
The given operator is a second-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={f}_{2}(x,y)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x,y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x,y)y
$$

with ${f}_{2}=y,{f}_{1}=-xy,$ and ${f}_{0}=5.$

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y={x}^{2}+1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}D({x}^{2}+1) & =({x}^{2}+1)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}({x}^{2}+1)-x({x}^{2}+1)\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}+1)+5({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x)-x({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2x+5({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2-2{x}^{2}({x}^{2}+1)+5({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =2({x}^{2}+1)-2{x}^{2}({x}^{2}+1)+5({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =7({x}^{2}+1)-2{x}^{2}({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)(7-2{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

q-338254:
The given operator is a third-order differential operator of the form

$$
D(y)={f}_{3}(x,y)\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}y}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}+{f}_{2}(x,y)\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+{f}_{1}(x,y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{f}_{0}(x,y)y
$$

with ${f}_{3}=xy,{f}_{2}=0,{f}_{1}=0,$ and ${f}_{0}=3.$

To compute $D(y),$ we apply the definition of the operator $D$ to the function $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡2x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}D(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x) & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\frac{{\text{d}}^{3}}{\text{d}{x}^{3}}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡2x\cdot (-8\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡2x(3-8x\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\end{aligned}
$$

q-130962:
First, we need to convert $Q$ to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -3 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -3 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{4} & :={R}_{4}+2{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -3 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Looking at the row echelon form, we see that $Q$ has $4$ pivots, and therefore the number of pivot columns is $4.$
